name: Agent framework libraries
vendor: Various (Microsoft, Pydantic, Hugging Face, OpenAI, AWS)
description: One entry for the class of agent frameworks that are imported libraries rather than installed applications - Semantic Kernel, PydanticAI, Smolagents, the OpenAI Agents SDK, Strands and their peers. They leave no dot-directory, no listener and no credential store of their own, so they are inventoried by pattern rather than by path.
execution_model: Imported library; agent loop and tool execution run inside the calling process
abuse_potential: These frameworks give arbitrary application code an agent loop with tool execution, without any of the install-time signals a packaged agent produces. A script that imports one and points it at a provider key has the same reach as a catalogued coding agent and none of its footprint. The credential is the caller's provider key rather than anything the framework owns, so credential theft here is theft of an environment variable.

disk.description: Presence in site-packages is the inventory signal for this class. It is evidence the library is available, not that an agent ran - absence of a dot-directory is expected here rather than suspicious. The same check applies to pydantic_ai, smolagents, agents (OpenAI Agents SDK) and strands.

Dependency manifests and lockfiles name the framework and pin its version, and they travel with the repository. Usually the fastest way to answer "was an agent framework in use here" across an estate, because it can be answered from source control rather than from endpoints.

network.indicator: Model provider API endpoints (api.openai.com, api.anthropic.com, generativelanguage.googleapis.com, api-inference.huggingface.co, bedrock-runtime.*.amazonaws.com)
network.description: Often the only network-visible signal, and the only one that distinguishes an installed library from a running agent. The destination identifies the provider; it does not identify which framework called it.

process.name: python
process.typical_parent: A shell, a scheduler, a CI runner or a service manager
process.typical_children: Whatever the agent's tools invoke - shells, interpreters, package managers. The child processes are the execution evidence, because the framework itself leaves none.
process.persistence: None - persistence belongs to whatever schedules the calling script

registry.description: The credential for this whole class. A persistently set user variable is the most common way a developer supplies it, and unlike a .env beside the script it is not tied to any one project.

credentials.location: OPENAI_API_KEY | ANTHROPIC_API_KEY | GOOGLE_API_KEY | HF_TOKEN | AWS credentials
credentials.description: The credential belongs to the calling code, not to the framework, and is almost always an environment variable or a .env file beside the script. This is shared across every framework in this class, which is why one entry covers them all.

collection.guidance: Inventory by pattern, not by path. Search dependency manifests and lockfiles first - it answers the question across an estate from source control without touching an endpoint. On a host, check site-packages for the module names and the process table for a Python process whose children are shells or package managers. Treat library presence as availability, not use: the evidence that an agent actually ran is the egress and the child processes, not the import. Collect the .env or environment beside the calling script, because the provider key there is the credential artifact for this whole class.

name: Docker Model Runner
description: Local model runner that ships with Docker Desktop and also runs standalone in Docker CE. Serves an OpenAI-compatible API. Unlike every other runtime in this catalog it can be present on a host where nobody chose to install a local LLM - it arrives with a tool the developer installed for unrelated reasons.
execution_model: Local inference served through the Docker socket, optionally on a host TCP port
abuse_potential: Reached through the Docker socket by default, so anything already able to talk to the socket can use it for free local inference without opening a port. When host-side TCP is enabled it becomes an unauthenticated OpenAI-compatible endpoint on the host. For shadow-AI inventory the question it raises is not "who installed a runtime" but "which of our Docker Desktop machines can serve models right now".

network.description: Present only when host-side TCP is enabled - `docker desktop enable model-runner --tcp 12434`. The /engines/v1, /models and /engines endpoints are served here. Absence of the port does not mean the runner is disabled, because the default path is the Docker socket instead.
Default access path. Anything with socket access can drive the runner, and socket access is already host-root-equivalent, so this is an escalation of an existing exposure rather than a new one.

process.name: model-runner
process.service_or_daemon: Standalone container in Docker CE, a Docker Desktop component elsewhere. On Desktop it sits inside the Desktop VM, so a host process listing may show nothing at all.

collection.guidance: Establish first whether the runner is enabled at all and whether host TCP is on, because the two have completely different exposure. Model storage is a named Docker volume, not a host path - enumerate it with `docker model ls` or the /models endpoint rather than looking for files. On Docker Desktop the runner lives inside the VM, so host process and file collection will miss it; the Docker API is the collection interface. Models live in a dedicated named volume rather than on the host filesystem - deliberate, so the runner can be uninstalled without re-pulling them, but it also means a filesystem sweep finds nothing.

name: Letta
description: Stateful agent framework. Agents live inside a Letta server and their memory is persisted to a database, so state survives process restarts and conversation resets - which makes it a persistence mechanism as well as a data store.
execution_model: Server-hosted agents with persistent memory, local or remote inference

The store may also contain whatever the agent was working on, which can include source code, retrieved documents and conversation content, so it carries handling implications of its own.

credentials.description: Plaintext Fernet key, written mode 0600, auto-generated on first vault use when LOCAL_CREDENTIAL_VAULT_KEY is unset. Decrypts every item in the local credential vault. These are the third-party website logins (usernames/passwords) and credit-card records that Skyvern replays into target sites during automated logins - i.e. The victim-relevant secrets, not Skyvern's own auth. This is the built-in vault used by default in the OSS docker-compose setup (CREDENTIAL_VAULT_TYPE=skyvern, ENABLE_LOCAL_CREDENTIAL_VAULT=true).

Container path of the local credential vault, set in the image and persisted by the compose file as host bind mount ./credential_vault. Contains both the encrypted creditem_*.bin files and the .fernet_key that decrypts them.

Plaintext env var supplying the vault Fernet key directly. When set, no .fernet_key file is generated - the key exists only in the process environment and in whatever .env or compose file provided it. Absence of .fernet_key alongside a populated vault means look here.

Plaintext backend env file at the repo/working root, created by `skyvern init` / `skyvern quickstart`. The CLI writes the generated SKYVERN_API_KEY into it directly, and it also carries the configured LLM provider keys (OPENAI_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, GEMINI_API_KEY, AZURE_API_KEY, OPENROUTER_API_KEY, GROQ_API_KEY, AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID / AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY) and POSTGRES_PASSWORD. Plaintext user-level backend env file (global scope). Skyvern layers a global ~/.skyvern env under the project-scope and repo-root .env files; which of them is consulted depends on the resolution intent, so this one is not always present or authoritative. Worth collecting when the repo-root .env does not explain the running configuration.

Plaintext frontend env file holding VITE_SKYVERN_API_KEY - the organization API key used by the UI. Vite bakes VITE_* values into the built bundle, so the key can also survive in the served JavaScript assets, not just this file.

Plaintext Bitwarden vault master password in an env var, used when CREDENTIAL_VAULT_TYPE=bitwarden. Plaintext 1Password service-account token in an env var, used when Skyvern is configured against a 1Password vault. Same escalation consideration as the Bitwarden variables - it reaches an external vault.

credentials.description: plaintext. The API key the server requires from clients, read from the process environment. Unset by default, which means no authentication at all. The --api-key CLI flag takes precedence over it, so check the command line as well as the environment before concluding the server was unauthenticated.
Plaintext Hugging Face token used to pull gated model weights, read from the environment. Grants access to whatever private repositories the account can reach.

collection.guidance: Establish the authentication posture first, because it decides whether this is an exposure: capture the full `vllm serve` command line and the process environment, and check for --api-key and VLLM_API_KEY together. Then confirm the bind address with `ss -lntp` rather than trusting the config - the default is 0.0.0.0. Collect ~/.config/vllm/usage_stats.json before any restart; it is often the only timeline of what was served. Note the model cache is shared with other Hugging Face consumers, so presence alone does not attribute activity to vLLM.

name: Warp
description: Agentic terminal. Every command, its output, exit code, working directory and timing is recorded in a local SQLite database rather than in a shell history file, and an in-terminal agent can propose and run commands.
execution_model: Cloud inference + local command execution in the user's shell
abuse_potential: The command database is a near-complete narrative of operator activity on the host, including commands typed into a pane and never saved to shell history, which makes it a collection target for an attacker as well as for a responder. The agent can also propose and execute commands, so a prompt-injection surface exists wherever it reads untrusted output.

disk.description: Command history, output, exit codes, working directories and timings. This is the highest-value artifact the tool produces and it has no shell-history equivalent - commands run in Warp do not reach .zsh_history. Collect the -wal and -shm siblings with it or recent activity is lost.

collection.guidance: Collect warp.sqlite together with its -wal and -shm siblings before the application is closed or the host is rebooted, or the most recent commands are lost. Treat the database as the primary execution timeline for this host - it records commands that never reach shell history. Cloud sync means the local copy may not be the whole record; scope the account as well as the endpoint.
